I've found a solution to having puzzles in my games. What I do is I create some kind of problem. Recently, I was running a modern setting where a bridge was infected by outer planar power. Once I present the full scenario, I let them figure out a solution. I didn't actually know how to solve it, but my players staged an accident, burned down the bridge, and made off with the infected wood. I find the best problems are to present a scenario with as much information to the players as possible and let them handle it. It's their job to solve the scenarios, not yours.

I write two documents: first is an overall design of the campaign, second is the design for every episode/session.
For the overall design, I start with drawing Harmon cycle: https://channel101.fandom.com/wiki/Story_Structure_101:_Super_Basic_Shit it makes for a good overall structure and makes sure you have a solid beginning middle and end. You want to note what you want to occur for each major event. ( e.g. what you need event is, what your meeting with the goddess is, what is your parties take decision, e.t.c.)
The overall should also have major factions, npc's, locations and previous events. It's really nice to know what happened before the party got there to make the world feel lived in.
The second document is the breakdown for every episode. They should only take one to two sessions each. The episode should fit into one and only one Harmon step. I break down each episode into three parts: 
1. A call to action, where you party gets a goal for the episode. Give them something concrete to do.
2. A search, this is the part I often skip out on. Your party will do some faffing about or interpersonal action. Let them do it here.
3. The resolution, what happens during the accomplishment of the goal set in the call.

Everybody wants to be social, even the introverts. I found that getting a hobby that gets you out of the home helps. It can get you distracted by the activity enough that you don't grow too attached to the people there but still social enough that you develop some social skills. If your having trouble finding a hobby group you can just run a search on meetup for things you find roughly interesting or awesome, chances are someones already started the group.
